content: Mammography screening programs for women over the age of 70 should be evaluated to determine the optimal screening interval and to assess the socioeconomic impact of expanding such programs to this older age group. This includes a thorough analysis of the benefits and harms associated with mammography screening in women aged 50–69 years, as well as research into the feasibility of implementing nationwide organized screening programs for this demographic. In settings with limited resources but relatively strong health systems, it is essential to evaluate the effectiveness of mammography screening programs, including the determination of the most appropriate screening intervals. Additionally, implementation research should be conducted to test the feasibility of establishing organized, population-based mammography screening programs for women aged 50–69 years. In resource-limited settings with either strong or weak health systems, alternative approaches to early detection of breast cancer should be explored. This includes validating low-cost screening methods and protocols that can be effectively implemented in such settings. The World Health Organization (WHO) plans to officially launch and disseminate its recommendations widely to regional and country offices, partners, governments, non-governmental organizations, technical agencies, and other stakeholders. A summary of the guidelines will also be published in a peer-reviewed journal. Furthermore, clear and simple messages targeting women and the general public will be developed and made available online. Mammography screening is recognized as cost-effective, feasible, and affordable, particularly in countries with well-established health infrastructure and comprehensive early detection programs. These programs must include quality assurance systems, accessible diagnostic and treatment facilities, and palliative care. Consequently, the implementation of these guidelines is primarily feasible in high-income and upper-middle-income countries. WHO, in collaboration with its partners, can support the implementation of these activities by providing practical tools and direct technical assistance when required. Multi-country demonstration projects of organized, population-based screening programs can be implemented, especially in upper-middle-income countries planning to develop effective programs. WHO and its partners will work with member states to evaluate the impact of the guidelines by coordinating efforts and providing advice and practical support. Tools and information systems will be developed to assess the impact of the guidelines, including performance indicators such as the dissemination and adoption of the recommendations within broader health policies and national cancer control programs. Countries with established screening programs or those developing demonstration programs will be advised to include process indicators (e.g., compliance with and timeliness of screening, diagnosis, and treatment, as well as quality assurance measures) and outcome indicators (e.g., stage distribution at diagnosis, survival rates, breast cancer mortality, interval cancer rates, and changes in public knowledge about the benefits and harms of mammography screening). Economic consequences should also be considered. The guidelines will be updated within five years to incorporate new knowledge, evidence-based information, national needs, and experiences. This ensures that the recommendations remain relevant and effective. Breast cancer is one of the most common cancers in women and a leading cause of death worldwide. Mammography screening is considered the most effective method for early detection of breast cancer. However, there is significant controversy regarding the balance of benefits and harms associated with mammography screening. This systematic review aims to summarize the best available evidence to inform the development of WHO guidance on this issue, assisting policymakers, patients, and healthcare providers in making informed decisions. The guidelines focus on optimal screening methods that are service-based, achieve high participation rates, and include established follow-up and quality assurance strategies. The systematic review follows an umbrella design, summarizing evidence from systematic reviews and evidence synthesis reports that evaluate mammography screening outcomes in women at average risk, regardless of study location or language. Eligible studies were identified through comprehensive database searches, expert consultations, and review of bibliographies. The most relevant reviews were selected based on comprehensiveness, recency, and quality, as assessed by the AMSTAR tool. Systematic reviews summarizing randomized trials generally had higher quality scores, while those summarizing observational studies had moderate scores or lacked sufficient detail for quality assessment. The selection, appraisal, and data extraction of systematic reviews were conducted by a single methodologist, ensuring a rigorous and consistent approach.
